title: A Parking Ticket Caught the Son of Sam

narration: For a year, police couldn't catch New York's most feared killer.
Then he parked by a fire hydrant.
shots.visual_description: ss12 street (night grade); ss12_officer: read -> present -> read; keyed camera moves, handheld; overlays: svg, label 'BROOKLYN · 31 JULY 1977', callout 'FIRE HYDRANT'.

sources.claim_text: Between July 1976 and July 1977 a gunman shot people in the Bronx, Queens and Brooklyn: six people were killed and seven wounded. He was arrested on 10 August 1977.

Police identified David Berkowitz through a parking ticket. After the last shooting (Brooklyn, 31 July 1977) detectives checked the parking tickets issued in the area that night; one, for a car parked too close to a fire hydrant, was for a 1970 Ford Galaxie registered to David Berkowitz of Yonkers, a 24-year-old postal employee. (The ticket amount, the street and the car's colour differ between sources and are not used.)

sources.claim_text: Between July 1976 and July 1977 a gunman shot people in the Bronx, Queens and Brooklyn: six people were killed and seven wounded. He was arrested on 10 August 1977.

narration: He wrote letters to police and the press.
He called himself the Son of Sam.
shots.visual_description: press hall (cold grade); press_operator: examine -> examine -> read_newspaper (walks); camera push/pull, handheld; overlays: label 'APRIL - MAY 1977', svg, card 'HE CALLED HIMSELF / 'SON OF SAM''.

sources.claim_text: In April 1977 a handwritten letter addressed to NYPD Captain Joseph Borrelli was left near a Bronx shooting, the first in which the killer called himself the 'Son of Sam'. On 30 May 1977 Daily News columnist Jimmy Breslin received a letter from him, which the paper published. (Letters not quoted in the episode.)

narration: He later claimed Sam was a neighbour whose dog relayed a demon's orders.
Then he admitted it was a hoax.
shots.visual_description: ss12 precinct (cold grade); detective: read -> stern -> stand; agent_a: arms_crossed -> hand_to_face -> arms_crossed; keyed camera moves, handheld; overlays: label 'AFTER HIS ARREST, HE CLAIMED...', funfact 'He later admitted the / 'demon dog' story / was a hoax.', stamp 'HOAX'.

sources.claim_text: FUN FACT: after his arrest Berkowitz claimed that a demon, speaking through his neighbour's dog, had ordered the killings. He later retracted it: a 1979 letter to his psychiatrist called it a hoax, and in 1980 interview tapes (used in the 2025 Netflix series) he said he made up the dog story.

narration: July 31st, 1977. His last attack, in Brooklyn.
shots.visual_description: ss12 street (night grade); ss12_witness (silhouette): stand (walks); camera push/pull, handheld; overlays: label 'BROOKLYN · 31 JULY 1977'.

sources.claim_text: The shooting on 31 July 1977 in Brooklyn was the last attack (and the first in Brooklyn).

narration: Nearby, a dog walker saw police ticketing a car.
It was parked by a fire hydrant.

sources.claim_text: A local woman walking her dog near the scene saw police ticketing a car parked by a fire hydrant, and reported it to police a few days later. Her name is spelled differently in different sources; she is not named in the episode.

narration: Days later, she told detectives.
They checked every ticket written there that night.

narration: In 1978, he pleaded guilty to all six murders.
25 years to life, for each one.

sources.claim_text: On 8 May 1978 he withdrew an insanity defence and pleaded guilty to the six murders; on 12 June 1978 he was sentenced to 25 years to life for each murder, to run consecutively (the maximum then allowed).

Berkowitz remains in a New York state prison. He was denied parole at every earlier hearing (the 12th denial was in May 2024); in May 2026 he declined to attend his parole hearing, saying he was not seeking release.

narration: New York passed a Son of Sam law against criminals profiting from their stories.
In 1991, the Supreme Court struck it down.

sources.claim_text: FUN FACT: in 1977 New York passed the 'Son of Sam law', which sent money a criminal earned from telling the story of the crime to the victims. In 1991 (Simon & Schuster v. Members of the New York State Crime Victims Board) the US Supreme Court held that version unconstitutional under the First Amendment; New York later enacted a revised law.
